title: Your uncle’s frozen Mac says it’s infected after viewing a Google ad. Now what?
gist: Netskope found a sophisticated tech-support scareware campaign delivered through Google Ads across 284+ legitimate publisher sites, using evasion techniques (mouse-movement triggers, in-memory decryption) that likely beat endpoint security and Google's ad filters; Google says it is investigating but gave no explanation of the miss.

insights.claim: Netskope tracked more than 250 Google Ads campaign IDs across at least 284 legitimate publisher sites delivering a tech-support scam that fakes a locked Windows or Mac screen and urges victims to call a bogus call center.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Malvertising slipping through Google's ad platform is a brand-safety and regulatory risk for Google's ad business and for publishers.

insights.claim: From August 31 to September 14, users at 619 Netskope customer organizations clicked the malicious ads, roughly 62 percent in the US followed by Japan and Australia, and actual exposure is likely much higher given Netskope's limited visibility.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Enterprise users are being exposed too, supporting demand for secure web gateway and cloud security vendors like Netskope.
insights.locator: The ads were displayed all over

insights.claim: Google said it has zero tolerance for scams and is investigating, but did not explain why its scanners missed the campaign or confirm the ads were fully removed; it says it blocked over 99 percent of violating ads before serving last year.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Gaps in Google's ad screening remain a recurring headline risk.

insights.claim: The scam kit only shows warnings after a mouse movement and is encrypted until decrypted in browser memory, conditions that prevent many endpoint security products and possibly Google's ad filters from detecting it.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Client-side evasion is outpacing static ad and endpoint scanning, favoring behavioral/network-level security approaches.

insights.claim: Scam victims can usually escape the fake lock by holding the Escape key for several seconds, or using Task Manager (Ctrl-Shift-Esc) on Windows or Force Quit (Cmd-Option-Esc) on Mac, and should never call the displayed number.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Practical user guidance; low investment relevance.
